questions.question: How does useState work and what are the common pitfalls?
questions.title: Use State Hook
questions.direct_answer: useState declares state that persists across renders. Calling the setter queues a re-render with the new value. Pitfalls: setter is asynchronous-looking (batched), stale closures capture old state, object state needs spreading (not mutation), and state from props should use a key-remount instead of syncing.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The hook state slot (the mechanism interviewers probe): each component instance has a slot list. useState registers slot 1 on first render and reads slot 1 on every render — the order of hooks must be stable across renders, which is WHY hooks can't be conditional or in loops. The state value lives in React's internal store keyed to the component instance, not in your closure.

The stale closure family (the bug class to enumerate): event handlers and effects capture the state at the render that created them. The symptom: a handler reads an old value after rapid updates. The three fixes: functional updates for the value itself, a ref (useRef) when you need the current value without re-rendering, or adding the value to the dependency array (in effects).

The derived-state anti-pattern (the design pitfall): copying props into state (`useState(props.value)`) breaks when props change — the state initialized once and never syncs. The correct pattern: derive during render, or use the key prop to remount the component when identity changes. If you truly need to 'reset on prop change,' the idiomatic answer is a keyed remount, not an effect that syncs.
